title: Bake the cake in the photo
allegory: Replicating a paper is like baking one cake from a famous bakery's book: follow the recipe card in your own kitchen, hold your cake up beside the photo, and write one honest note on what matched and what the photo never promised.

cap.1: A paper arrives with many figures and a wall of claims. Try to rebuild all of it in three Saturdays and you finish none of it.
cap.2: The capstone is three Saturdays, and week 12 is already project time. Scope is the first decision: one figure fully reproduced beats five half-reproduced.
cap.3: Replication effort scales with every unstated detail you must rediscover. Scoping to a single figure bounds that search and makes a clean positive or negative result possible.

cap.1: Pick one cake from the bakery's book. Follow the recipe card, bake it in your own kitchen, then hold your cake up beside the photo. That is a replication.
cap.2: One paper, one figure: rerun the method with your own code, plot your result on the same axes and metric as the paper, and compare them side by side.
cap.3: A replication fixes the target (one figure), the protocol (the paper's methods) and the comparison (same axes, same metric), so any difference is attributable and reportable.

cap.1: Start from a chapter 4 section: each is built around one or two recent papers, with the rebuilding half already set up for you.
cap.2: ARENA's chapter 4 sections are the shortest path from a paper to a result you can present: the replication is scaffolded, so your Saturdays go on the comparison and the claim.
cap.3: Scaffolded replications strip out boilerplate risk and leave the scientific part: matching the figure and characterising where, and why, it diverges.

cap.1: Lay your curve over theirs. Close is a result. A gap is a clue: a missing setting, a different seed, a different model.
cap.2: Plot on the paper's axes and metric. When you diverge, first check seeds and settings the paper mentions only in passing; a gap that survives that is itself a finding.
cap.3: Divergence decomposes into implementation error, unreported degrees of freedom and genuine non-robustness. Separate them with seeds and targeted ablations before concluding anything.

chapters.name: One honest line
chapters.verdict: Say what it shows, and one thing it does not.

cap.1: The last step is one sentence about your cake. 'Rose as promised, only tried at sea level' is worth more than 'perfect cake'.
cap.2: Write the claim you can defend: which figure reproduced, on which model and settings, plus one thing the result does not show, such as generality beyond that setup.
cap.3: Bound the claim by the evidence: setup, seeds, what matched and what did not, and an explicit non-claim. Honest scoping is what lets others build on your replication.

cap.1: What we believe about how AI works rests on papers. Rebuilding one figure yourself teaches you the method and shows you how solid the claim is.
cap.2: Interpretability and alignment results steer what the field builds next. A careful replication with an honest caveat is a real contribution, and a talk you can give.
cap.3: Replication turns reading into method: you learn the pipeline, its failure points and the evidential weight of the claim, which is what understanding and steering models requires.

coda.title: Is your gap real, or seed luck?

curves.label: where your true average could be

readouts.label: verdict
readouts.f: abs(m - 0.8) > 2 * s / sqrt(n) ? 'a real gap: hunt for the missing detail' : 'within noise: consistent with the paper'

caption.1: Your one-seed score is 0.74 against the paper's 0.80. Is that gap real? Add seeds and watch the bell narrow until you can tell.
caption.2: Averaging n seeds shrinks the wobble by √n. A gap bigger than about two standard errors is unlikely to be luck; that is when you go hunting for the missing detail.
caption.3: SE = s/√n, and |gap| > 2·SE is a rough 95% rule under a normal approximation. It ignores the paper's own uncertainty: if they report error bars, compare against those too.

Code review and audits: rebuild a claim before you build on it
Capability evals, where a number means little until someone else can reproduce it
Any lab science, where one careful replication beats a broad, shaky one

hamming.what: Reproducing one figure from one paper with your own code, then stating one honest thing about what it does and doesn't show.
hamming.when: In the capstone (three Saturdays, from week 12), and whenever you want to build on a result you have not checked.
hamming.why: Results about models are easy to overread; rebuilding one figure teaches you the method and shows exactly where the claim is solid.

object.title: The side-by-side light table
object.subtitle: The paper's figure in the front row, your replication behind it, the same points on the same axes.

cap.1: Two rows of bars: the paper's figure in front, yours behind. Same points, same axes, so any difference jumps out.
cap.2: Your result plotted on the paper's axes and metric, point for point.
cap.3: A paired comparison at matched x-values: the only honest way to call a replication close or not.

cap.1: With one seed your bars wobble up and down. You cannot yet tell a real gap from luck.
cap.2: A single seed mixes the true difference with run-to-run noise.
cap.3: One run's deviation is signal plus seed variance; with n = 1 you cannot separate them.

cap.1: Average nine seeds and the wobble shrinks to a third. A steady gap remains: yours sits lower almost everywhere.
cap.2: Averaging n seeds shrinks noise by √n. What is left is a systematic gap worth explaining.
cap.3: With noise down by √9 = 3, the residual is a consistent multiplicative shortfall: a protocol difference, not chance.

cap.1: Find the missing detail, a setting the paper stated only in passing, and the rows line up.
cap.2: Closing the gap by fixing one setting tells you that setting matters, which is itself worth reporting.
cap.3: A targeted change that closes the gap is an ablation result: it identifies a sensitivity the paper under-emphasised.

cap.1: Now write the one honest line: what matched, what did not, and what this figure never showed.
cap.2: Report the setup, the seeds, the gap you closed and how, and a clear non-claim.
cap.3: Scope the conclusion to the setup tested; state an explicit non-claim, such as generality to other models.

predict.q: Your one-seed replication lands a bit below the paper. What do you do first?

options.t: Run more seeds to see whether the gap is real
Announce that the paper is wrong

predict.why: One seed cannot separate a real gap from luck; averaging n seeds shrinks the noise by √n.

predict.q: Everything matches. What is the honest claim?

options.t: This figure reproduces on this setup; it does not show the result is general

predict.why: A replication checks one figure under one setup. Say what it shows and one thing it does not.
